sections.title: Use a situation you can revisit

paragraphs.text: You can use this book one question at a time. Choose an ordinary situation you feel comfortable revisiting, including one involving your own behaviour. The aim is to leave with a better question or a considered action, rather than a label for a person.

Listen to the explanation first. Brief fictional examples show how a distinction might work, but they do not demonstrate that a method succeeds. Try a relevant exercise when it helps. You do not need to complete every exercise or analyse every interaction.

The chapters build a sequence from interpreting behaviour to choosing what to do. The reference library lets you explore a particular concept more deeply. Reading, listening and practice sit together within each entry. The practice section of the book helps you choose an exercise, and the supporting pages explain sources and evidence standards.

If a term is unfamiliar, its explanation and the glossary can help. Research links stay beside the claims they support. Longer exercises and further comparisons are optional, so you can follow the main explanation without opening everything.

After a chapter, try recalling its central question without looking back. Then consider the fresh fictional situation before checking the suggested answer. Your wording can differ. Compare the reasoning: did you separate observation from explanation, recognise an important uncertainty, and choose something you could actually do?

Next, apply the idea once during the week. Include what you said or did, not just the other person’s response. Return later and ask what you learned. The exercises are self-checks, not scored tests or evidence that you will remember the material in future.
You can revisit the recall question a week later. The conclusion also gathers the main questions when you want a refresher. There is no need to keep a running assessment of everyone around you.

sections.title: Keep notes only if useful and safe

paragraphs.text: You can record a short description, your explanation and what remains unknown in your own notebook or the page’s optional note fields. With JavaScript available, those fields save in this browser on this device. They do not sync between devices, send reminders or send your notes to the author.

Anyone using the same browser may be able to read the notes. Avoid names and sensitive details, and do not keep records if their discovery could put you at risk. Private browsing or clearing browser data can remove saved notes. Downloading a copy keeps a separate file; deleting notes from the page does not delete that copy.

If saving is blocked, copy or download anything you want before leaving. Without JavaScript, the fields do not save. Notes are optional throughout; remembering one useful question is a perfectly reasonable way to use the book.

sections.title: Understand the limits and choose a next step

paragraphs.text: The practical framework and worksheet bring together ideas from the book. Researchers have not tested them as a complete method. They are not tools for diagnosis, treatment, personality testing or establishing guilt. The complete first draft has not had external subject-matter review, and its sources are a selective collection.

Uncertainty does not require endless delay. You can change an arrangement after repeated missed commitments without settling someone’s motives. You also do not have to keep searching for an innocent explanation of harmful conduct. Acknowledging uncertainty can sit alongside a clear response to its effects.

For your next lesson, choose one event, one question and one opportunity to review what happened. If you return to notes, check whether your explanation changed and whether your own action helped. That small cycle is enough; more analysis is useful only when it improves the next decision.
